chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
You may also be more likely to have PMOS if a close relative has it or you are from an Asian
background. Complications of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) can sometimes increase the risk of serious
conditions, including:
type 2 diabetes (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/type-2-diabetes/)
high blood pressure (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/high-blood-pressure/)
cardiovascular disease (CVD) (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/cardiovascular-disease/)
non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/non-alcoholic-fatty-liverdisease/)
womb (uterus) cancer (Link: www.nhs.uk/conditions/womb-cancer/)
You can reduce the risk of developing these conditions by getting regular check-ups. Talk to
your doctor if you're worried. Help and support for polyendocrine metabolic
ovarian syndrome (PMOS)
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) can be a difficult condition to live with,
both physically and emotionally. As well as support from your doctor, you may find it helpful to get support from charities,
organisations and other people with PMOS.

chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
The main symptoms of PMOS include:
irregular periods or long gaps between your periods
excessive hair growth (hirsutism) (Link: www.nhs.uk/symptoms/hirsutism/) or hair loss
weight gain or difficulty losing weight
difficulty getting pregnant
mental health problems, such as depression or anxiety
oily skin and acne
feeling very tired
thick, dark patches of skin on the neck or armpits (acanthosis nigricans (Link:
www.nhs.uk/conditions/acanthosis-nigricans/))
When and where to get medical help
Some of the symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) are common
and can be caused by many different conditions. Having them does not definitely mean you
have PMOS, but it's important to get them checked. (Link: www.nhs.uk/)

chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is a hormone condition that can affect
hair growth, periods, fertility and mood. There is no cure, but treatments and lifestyle
changes can help. PMOS used to be called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
Symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) usually start in girls and
young women under the age of 18, at puberty, and continue until menopause. It can affect
anyone who has ovaries. After menopause, some symptoms will stop or may change. Symptoms can be mild or severe, or you may have no symptoms at all.

chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
Tests for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
If a GP thinks you have polyendocrine metabolic syndrome (PMOS), they may arrange tests
with a reproduction or hormone specialist (gynaecologist or endocrinologist). Tests for PMOS include:
blood tests to check hormone levels and insulin resistance
an ultrasound scan (Link: www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/ultrasound-scan/) to look at
your ovaries
An ultrasound scan will only be done if you are over 18 years old. Treatments for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
There is no cure for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), but there are
treatments and lifestyle changes that can help your symptoms.

chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
Surgery for PMOS fertility problems
PMOS can sometimes cause problems getting pregnant. This is usually because the ovaries do
not release an egg each month. If you've tried other PMOS treatments or lifestyle changes that have not worked, a doctor
may suggest a procedure called laparoscopic ovarian drilling. This uses heat or laser to remove tissue on your ovaries and may help release more eggs. This
can sometimes increase the chance of getting pregnant. Things you can do to help polyendocrine
metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS)
If you have polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), there are things you can do
to help your symptoms. NHS help to get healthy
NHS Better Health has free tools and support to help you lose weight and get active. Visit the NHS Better Health website (Link: https://www.nhs.uk/better-health/)
Causes of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian
The cause of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is unknown, but it may be
to do with hormones such as insulin and testosterone not working properly.

chunks.title: PCOS – NHS Overview
chunks.text:
Medicines for PMOS
PMOS symptoms are sometimes treated with:
the combined pill (Link: www.nhs.uk/contraception/methods-of-contraception/combinedpill/), progestogen-only pill (Link: www.nhs.uk/contraception/methods-ofcontraception/progestogen-only-pill/) or an intrauterine system (IUS) (Link:
www.nhs.uk/contraception/methods-of-contraception/ius-hormonal-coil/), to help with
irregular periods
clomifene, a medicine used to improve fertility
spironolactone (Link: www.nhs.uk/medicines/spironolactone/) or eflornithine to help
reduce hair growth on the face and body
weight loss medicines if you're overweight
metformin (Link: www.nhs.uk/medicines/metformin/), a type 2 diabetes medicine to help
tiredness and weight problems
skins creams or tablets that can help acne
